newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Yeltsin prepares to meet China leader.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Yeltsin prepares to meet China leader.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, fresh from a visit to Germany overshadowed by NATO expansion plans, prepared on Monday for talks with Chinese President Jiang Zemin on further rapprochement between the two states.

A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin, who retreated for a short holiday in the Black Sea resort of Sochi after last week's talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, would spend the day making final preparations for Jiang's visit which starts on Tuesday.

He said the president was expected to fly to Moscow to meet Jiang and sign a five-sided treaty on cutting troops along the former Soviet-Chinese border. The leaders of Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan will also sign the pact.
The spokesman did not say when Yeltsin, 66, who had heart surgery last November, would resume his holiday in Sochi.
Yeltsin and the Chinese leader, who will meet on Wednesday, are also due to sign a bilateral political declaration outlining their vision of world order in the next century.
This would be the first such declaration signed by Beijing and Moscow since they started improving their relations in the late 1980s after more than two decades of hostility.

"In this declaration...Russia and China will express their vision of how to form the new international order in the 21st century and will speak out against claims by any country to the role of absolute leader," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying.

Yastrzhembsky, who did not name a specific country, was clearly referring to Moscow's worries about U.S.-led plans to grant NATO membership to some of the former Soviet Union's one-time allies in the old Warsaw Pact.
Russia views NATO expansion as a threat to European stability and an attempt to marginalise Moscow.
Yeltsin told Kohl on Thursday that he would sign a deal with NATO on future relations on May 27, hoping to minimise Russia's losses from the expansion.

But Russian officials have made clear that Moscow is seeking new allies as a counter-balance to the Western alliance. Russia sees China, which is at odds with the West over human rights violations, as a priority partner.

Russian and Chinese officials have cited the border treaty as an example of a new concept of maintaining regional security through confidence-building measures rather than through expanding military blocks.
But no details of the pact have been revealed and some officials said it could be kept classified even after signing.
Moscow, where consumers have started shunning cheap and often poorly-made Chinese goods, also expects Jiang's visit could help further boost bilateral trade.
"Chinese produce wonderful goods which go to the West but they continue supplying us with far worse stuff," one government expert told Reuters.
"This stuff doesn't sell in Russia and the Chinese have to understand that they have to change their approach if they want to expand on Russian market."
Russia also hopes to boost arms sales to China from current levels of around $1 billion a year. Some estimates say this could be up to 30 percent of Moscow's overall arms exports.
